body.text: Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese, right, takes a selfie with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi at the Australia-India Economic Roadmap Business Reception in Melbourne, 9 July 2026 (William West/AFP via Getty Images)
An AI agenda for the India-Australia partnership
Australia has data centre capacity to spare and India has AI demand it cannot meet – the two lack only a way to match them.

Australia is building data centre capacity at a pace it cannot absorb, while India’s AI expansion requires computing power on a scale it cannot build fast enough – creating a natural complementarity both countries can take advantage of.

The Australian National AI Plan, released in December 2025, presents Australia as the Indo-Pacific’s home for trusted digital infrastructure, citing more than A$100 billion in forecast data centre investment alongside an abundant renewable resource. It also instructs Austrade to market the country as a regional AI hub, including a mandate to find demand in other regions. India offers a suitable destination.

Indian businesses are adopting AI at some of the highest rates and demand is outrunning what can be built domestically. This offers a chance to outsource the infrastructure – training a large model is a kind of workload where the physical distance is immaterial.

Other governments are bidding for the same business. India and the United Arab Emirates agreed terms in May 2026 for a cluster involving G42 and the Centre for Development of Advanced Computing. However, this was a single transaction with no standing framework behind it.
Governments planning around a rule set that moves will look for partners they can rely on, and reliability is what the Australian relationship supplies.

Japan is the more instructive case. A week before Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s visit to Melbourne in July, India and Japan issued a joint statement on AI, having convened the first round of a dedicated AI Strategic Dialogue in April and agreed to hold further rounds regularly. That dialogue covers data centres, compute and semiconductors, which is close to the agenda Canberra and New Delhi have left unattended.

Australia still provides a better case – with surplus land, renewable energy, and a data centre sector still drawing about 2% of national electricity. Energy ministers agreed this year that new data centres must fund additional renewable generation to cover what they consume. Underwriting new generation is financeable only against long-term contracted demand, which could be supplied through a substantial Indian commitment.

Governments planning around a rule set that moves will look for partners they can rely on, and reliability is what the Australian relationship supplies. By contrast, American policy on exporting AI components, has proved changeable. The diffusion rule that placed India in a capped tier was scrapped in May 2025 before it took effect, and a Commerce Department draft that would have required case-by-case approval for almost every advanced accelerator leaving the country was circulated in February 2026 and shelved a month later. India’s access today is good, though it rests on a position that has already been reversed once and redrafted twice.

The most valuable early project for Australia and India would cost comparatively little. AI models are still evaluated overwhelmingly in English, so a model that performs respectably in English can fail badly in Hindi, Tamil or Bengali without the standard test suites registering it. India has 22 official languages and a government pushing AI into public services delivered in all of them, which gives it both the problem and the data. Australia has a new AI safety institute, a seat in the international network of such institutes, and no equivalent test set of its own. Shared benchmarks for multilingual and Indic-language models would be technically achievable and useful to both governments, and no commercial developer has much reason to fund them.

Both countries also have a similar approach to regulation – favouring guidelines over hard law. Both governments looked hard at binding AI rules, and both drew back within the same 12 months, India declining a standalone AI law in favour of the governance guidelines it published in November 2025, and Australia changing its proposed mandatory guardrails when the National AI Plan appeared. Each now runs a safety institute that tests and advises without holding regulatory powers.

What the relationship lacks is machinery. The meeting between Modi and Australia’s Anthony Albanese in July 2026 launched the Australia-India Partnership on Cyber, Critical Technologies and Supply Chains, organised across five pillars and overseen at deputy national security adviser level. AI appears as one of five technologies inside one of those pillars. While this is a defensible way to file the subject it is a thin way to pursue it, because a line item inside one of five pillars competes for money and ministerial attention with everything listed alongside it. A dedicated mechanism acquires its own calendar and its own officials, whose job it is to produce results. India drew that distinction with Japan a week earlier.

An annual India-Australia AI dialogue, carved out of the critical technology pillar and given standing of its own, would supply what is missing, with the language benchmarks as a first task and the harder negotiation over compute access as its eventual purpose. The relationship has spent a decade closing its most difficult legacy files with nuclear cooperation. This would be the best time to start cooperating on what will become one of the most defining technologies for the next decade.
Nidhi Singh is an associate fellow at Carnegie India. Her current research interests include data governance, artificial intelligence and emerging technologies.
